draft.title: Chemical tests for organic compounds
card: A functional group is the part of an organic molecule that gives it its typical reactions. A simple test on a small sample can show which group is present.
Orange-brown bromine water is shaken with the sample. If it turns colourless, the molecule has a C=C double bond (it is unsaturated). A saturated alkane does not decolourise it quickly in the dark.
Sodium carbonate is added to the sample. If bubbles of carbon dioxide gas form, a carboxylic acid is present. Alcohols do not give bubbles.
A test gives a positive result only for its own group. Using several tests on one sample, and ruling groups in or out, narrows down what the compound could be.
draft.remember: Bromine water losing its colour points to a C=C bond. Fizzing with sodium carbonate points to a carboxylic acid.

a.q: A student adds orange-brown bromine water to a liquid, and the mixture quickly turns colourless. What does this show?
opts: The liquid has a C=C double bond
The liquid has a carboxylic acid group
The liquid is a saturated hydrocarbon
The liquid has no functional group
a.why: Bromine adds across a C=C double bond, so the orange-brown colour disappears. A saturated hydrocarbon would leave the colour in place, so it is not the answer.
a.clue: Which group makes the bromine water lose its colour?

b.q: Sample X is a colourless liquid. It gives bubbles when sodium carbonate is added, and bromine water stays orange-brown. Which compound could X be?
b.why: Bubbles show a carboxylic acid, and no colour change shows there is no C=C bond, so propanoic acid fits. Propenoic acid is the tempting option, but it has a C=C bond and would decolourise bromine water.
b.clue: Use both results: one test rules a group in, the other rules one out.

a.best: The liquid has a C=C double bond

problems.detail: "A test gives a positive result only for its own group" is an overclaim. Bromine water is also decolourised by C≡C triple bonds (and oxidised by aldehydes). Sodium carbonate fizzes with any acid stronger than carbonic acid, not just carboxylic acids. Saying a positive result "suggests" or "points to" a group, as the remember line does, would be accurate.

check.summary: Both questions are sound, each with one clear answer. The card's claim that each test is positive "only" for its own group overstates things: triple bonds also decolourise bromine water, and other acids fizz with carbonate. It should be softened.

proposal.title: Chemical tests for organic compounds
card: A functional group is the part of an organic molecule that gives it its typical reactions. A simple test on a small sample can show which groups are likely present.

Orange-brown bromine water is shaken with the sample. If it quickly turns colourless, the molecule is likely unsaturated, with a C=C or C≡C bond. A saturated alkane does not decolourise it quickly in the dark.
Sodium carbonate is added to the sample. If bubbles of carbon dioxide gas form, an acid such as a carboxylic acid is likely present. Alcohols do not give bubbles.
A positive result suggests a group but does not prove it, as some other groups can react too. Using several tests on one sample, and ruling groups in or out, narrows down what the compound could be.
proposal.remember: Bromine water losing its colour points to a C=C bond. Fizzing with sodium carbonate points to a carboxylic acid.

a.clue: What kind of bond makes bromine water lose its colour?
